title: Graeci Aulide. Fama
titleEn: The Greeks Held at Aulis; the House of Rumour — Metamorphoses XII.1–63
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Priam mourns Aesacus, not knowing that he lives on with wings, and Paris is absent from the funeral rites — the man whose carrying-off of a wife will bring a long war home. Wind and the Boeotian coast pin the Greek fleet at Aulis, where a snake devours eight nestlings and their mother in a plane tree standing next to the rites just begun; the son of Thestor reads the nine birds as nine years of war, and the snake is turned to stone. When the sea's anger will not fall, the seer names the price: the virgin goddess must be appeased with a virgin's blood, and Iphigenia stands at the altar, though a hind is said to have been put in her place. The fleet takes the Phrygian shore, and the scene shifts to the house of Rumour, a building of sounding bronze at the meeting-point of earth, sea and sky, open night and day, where invented things circulate mixed in with true ones.

sentences.t:
Nescius adsumptis Priamus pater Aesacon alis
vivere lugebat, tumulo quoque nomen habenti
inferias dederat cum fratribus Hector inani.
sentences.l:
Not knowing that Aesacus lived, wings taken on, Priam the father
was mourning; and at a tomb that also bore his name,
an empty one, Hector with his brothers had given the offerings of the dead.
sentences.i: Priam his father, not knowing that Aesacus was alive and winged, mourned him as dead; and Hector with his brothers had made the offerings owed the dead at an empty tomb that carried his name.
sentences.n: “nescius” takes an accusative and infinitive here — “Aesacon … vivere”, “that Aesacus was living”. “adsumptis … alis” is an ablative absolute, “with wings taken on”: the son Priam is mourning has become a bird. “Aesacon” is the Greek accusative of the name. “inferias” are the offerings made to the dead, and “tumulo … inani” is a cenotaph, a tomb with nothing in it. “quoque” here is the plain adverb “also” — the empty mound has his name on it as well. Magnus prints “inani” with the tomb, “an empty tomb”; some editions print “inanes”, which attaches the emptiness instead to the offerings. “adsumptis” keeps the unassimilated spelling of the edition and is not an error.

sentences.i: Paris was not there for the grim rite — the man who later, with the wife he had carried off, brought a long war home upon his own country;
sentences.n: “officio … tristi” is dative with “defuit”: the presence “was lacking to” the sad service, the funeral just described. “qui” is an ordinary relative pronoun whose antecedent is the genitive “Paridis”, so English has to supply a noun for it to hang on — “the man who”. “rapta cum coniuge” is not an ablative absolute but an ordinary accompaniment phrase, “along with the wife who had been carried off”; the woman is named nowhere in this part, and here Paris' city is called only “patria”, his own country. “postmodo” = afterwards.

sentences.t:
coniurataeque sequuntur
mille rates gentisque simul commune Pelasgae.
sentences.l:
and there follow, sworn together,
a thousand ships, and at the same time the joint force of the Pelasgian race.
sentences.i: and a thousand ships, bound by a common oath, come after him, and with them the whole muster of the Pelasgian nation.
sentences.n: “coniuratae” describes the ships by the oath their crews swore together. “rates” (properly rafts) is standard verse for ships. “commune” is the neuter adjective used as a noun, “the thing held in common” — the joint undertaking or combined strength of the “gens Pelasga”; Pelasgi is one of the poem's old-sounding names for the Greeks at large, and the seer uses it again in his address below. “sequuntur” is deponent — passive in form, active in sense — and its present tense drops the narrative into the historic present, which quickens the pace after the past tenses of the lines before.

sentences.t:
Nec dilata foret vindicta, nisi aequora saevi
invia fecissent venti Boeotaque tellus
Aulide piscosa puppes tenuisset ituras.
sentences.l:
Nor would the vengeance have been put off, had not the savage
winds made the seas impassable, and the Boeotian land
held back at fish-teeming Aulis the ships that were about to go.
sentences.i: And the reckoning would not have been delayed, if the fierce winds had not made the sea impassable and the land of Boeotia had not held the ships at fish-rich Aulis just as they were about to sail.
sentences.n: A past condition contrary to fact: “foret” (an older form of “esset”) with the pluperfect subjunctives “fecissent” and “tenuisset” — “would not have been … if they had not”. “saevi … venti” is pulled apart, the adjective closing one line and its noun waiting in the next, a stretch hexameter makes routine. “ituras” is the future participle, “on the point of going”. “Aulide” is the ablative of Aulis, the Boeotian harbour; “piscosa” (full of fish) is a flat descriptive epithet, the harbour as a fisherman would know it.

sentences.t:
Hic patrio de more Iovi cum sacra parassent,
ut vetus accensis incanduit ignibus ara,
serpere caeruleum Danai videre draconem
in platanum, coeptis quae stabat proxima sacris.
sentences.l:
Here, when after their fathers' custom they had prepared rites for Jupiter,
as the ancient altar whitened with the kindled fires,
the Danaans saw a dark-blue serpent creeping
into a plane tree, which stood nearest to the rites begun.
sentences.i: There, when they had made the sacrifice ready for Jupiter in their fathers' way, and the old altar had gone white with the kindled fire, the Greeks saw a blue-black snake climbing into a plane tree that stood closest to the rites they had just begun.
sentences.n: “parassent” is syncopated for “paravissent” — a contraction verse takes freely, not a fault in the text. “videre” is “viderunt”, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ēre; you meet it again a few lines down in “obstipuere”. “serpere … draconem” is accusative and infinitive after a verb of perceiving: they saw the serpent creeping. “incanduit” is to go white with heat. “caeruleum” runs from dark blue to blue-green — the colour of sea water and of snakes. “Danai”, the Danaans, is another of the poem's names for the Greeks.

sentences.t: Nidus erat volucrum bis quattuor arbore summa:
sentences.l: There was a nest of twice four birds at the top of the tree:
sentences.i: At the top of the tree was a nest with twice four birds in it:
sentences.n: “bis quattuor”, twice four, is the poets' way of saying eight; verse likes a small multiplication where prose gives the figure flat. Count them as Ovid does: eight nestlings here, and the mother taken with them in the next line makes nine — the number the seer works with below. “arbore summa” is ablative of place without a preposition, and “summus” means the top part of a thing, so it is the tree's crown, not a tall tree.

sentences.t:
quas simul et matrem circum sua damna volantem
corripuit serpens avidoque recondidit ore.
sentences.l:
which, together with the mother flying around her own losses,
the serpent snatched up and stowed away in its greedy mouth.
sentences.i: and the snake seized them, and the mother too as she flew round her own loss, and put them away in its greedy mouth.
sentences.n: “quas” is a connecting relative, feminine accusative plural picking up the birds, so English wants “and them”. “sua damna”, her own losses, stands in for the nestlings themselves: the mother is circling not her young but the loss of them, a hard little substitution of the abstract for the living. “recondidit” is the verb of putting something away out of sight, which is what a swallowing mouth does.

sentences.t: Obstipuere omnes.
sentences.l: They were all struck dumb.
sentences.i: Every one of them stood stunned.
sentences.n: “obstipuere” is “obstipuerunt”, the -ēre perfect again (compare “videre” above). The verb is of being rooted where you stand by shock. Two words make the whole sentence: the crowd's reaction gets its own beat before the seer is allowed to speak.

sentences.t:
At veri providus augur
Thestorides “vincemus” ait, “gaudete, Pelasgi!
sentences.l:
But the augur foreseeing the truth,
Thestor's son, “we shall conquer,” he says, “rejoice, Pelasgians!
sentences.i: But the seer who saw the truth coming, the son of Thestor, said, “We shall win — rejoice, Pelasgians!
sentences.n: “veri providus” — “foreseeing of the truth”: the adjective takes a genitive of the thing foreseen. “Thestorides” is a patronymic, “son of Thestor”, the standard way of naming the Greek army's prophet Calchas; the Latin here uses only the patronymic and never the name. The speaker is named first, by his patronymic, and the verb of speaking is dropped in after the opening word of the speech rather than before it, so that the one-word promise “vincemus” lands before anything else and the rest of the speech follows “ait”. Present “ait” beside future “vincemus”.

sentences.t: Troia cadet, sed erit nostri mora longa laboris,”
sentences.l: Troy will fall, but the delay of our toil will be long,”
sentences.i: Troy will fall; but there will be a long wait before our work is done.”
sentences.n: “mora … laboris” is “a delay of the toil”: the genitive says what is being held up, so the claim is that the army's work will be long in reaching its end. The two plain futures “cadet” and “erit” give the prophecy its shape — certainty about the outcome, vagueness about the time. The number itself comes in the line after, and not in the seer's mouth: the closing quotation mark ends his speech here, and it is the narrator who reports what he does with the birds.

sentences.t: atque novem volucres in belli digerit annos.
sentences.l: and he distributes the nine birds into years of war.
sentences.i: and he parcels the nine birds out into that many years of war.
sentences.n: “digerit … in annos” is to sort or distribute into: the seer turns each bird into a year. The arithmetic is all in the text — eight nestlings (“bis quattuor”) plus the mother snatched with them, and Ovid states the total himself as “novem”, nine. The present tense keeps the reading happening in front of us rather than reported after the fact.

sentences.t:
Ille, ut erat virides amplexus in arbore ramos,
fit lapis et servat serpentis imagine saxum.
sentences.l:
He, just as he was, having wrapped the green branches on the tree,
becomes stone, and the rock keeps him in the likeness of a serpent.
sentences.i: The snake, still coiled as he was about the green branches in the tree, turns to stone, and the rock holds him in a serpent's shape.
sentences.n: “ut erat”, “just as he was”, freezes the posture along with the creature. “amplexus” is the perfect participle of the deponent “amplector”, so it is active in force — having embraced, not having been embraced. “serpentis imagine” is ablative: the rock preserves him in the form of a snake. The portent ends as its own monument: the creature that gave the sign is fixed in the posture it held while giving it.

sentences.t:
Permanet Aoniis Nereus violentus in undis
bellaque non transfert;
sentences.l:
Nereus goes on violent in the Aonian waves
and does not carry the war across;
sentences.i: The sea stays rough in the waters of Boeotia and will not ferry the war across;
sentences.n: Nereus, the old sea-god, stands by metonymy for the sea itself, so “violentus” is really the roughness of the water. “Aoniis” is Boeotian — Aonia is the poets' name for the region Aulis lies in. “transfert” is literally “carries across”: the sea will not move the war from one shore to the other. Magnus prints “Nereus”; some editions print “Boreas”, which makes the North Wind rather than the sea the thing refusing them passage.

sentences.t:
et sunt qui parcere Troiae
Neptunum credant, quia moenia fecerat urbi.
sentences.l:
and there are those who would believe that Neptune spares Troy,
because he had made walls for the city.
sentences.i: and there are some who think Neptune is sparing Troy, because he had built the city its walls.
sentences.n: “sunt qui … credant” with the subjunctive describes a type of person rather than named men, and it lets Ovid report a belief without standing behind it. “parcere … Neptunum” is accusative and infinitive inside that belief, with “parcere” taking the dative “Troiae”. “moenia fecerat urbi” — the walls of Troy were Neptune's work, and the pluperfect puts that far back behind the present standoff.

sentences.t: At non Thestorides:
sentences.l: But not Thestor's son:
sentences.i: Not so the son of Thestor:
sentences.n: The verb has to be carried over from the sentence before: not so the seer — he is not one of those who think that. Ovid marks him off by the patronymic a second time rather than by a name, and the edition's colon leaves him standing there while the next clause says what he does instead.

sentences.t:
nec enim nescitve tacetve
sanguine virgineo placandam virginis iram
esse deae.
sentences.l:
for he neither is ignorant nor keeps silent
that with virgin blood the anger of the virgin
goddess must be appeased.
sentences.i: for he neither fails to know it nor keeps it to himself: the anger of the virgin goddess has to be appeased with a virgin's blood.
sentences.n: “nec … nescitve … tacetve” piles negatives: he does not either not-know or say nothing — a double denial that insists he both knows and speaks. “placandam … esse” is the passive periphrastic, the construction of what must be done. The force of the sentence is in the pairing “sanguine virgineo … virginis”: the virgin blood demanded and the virgin who demands it are set side by side. The goddess herself is not named until later in the passage.

sentences.t:
Postquam pietatem publica causa
rexque patrem vicit castumque datura cruorem
flentibus ante aram stetit Iphigenia ministris,
sentences.l:
After the public cause had conquered family duty,
and the king the father, and, about to give her chaste blood,
Iphigenia stood before the altar, the attendants weeping,
sentences.i: When the public cause had overcome a father's duty to his own, and the king in him had overcome the father, and Iphigenia stood at the altar ready to give her chaste blood, with the attendants in tears,
sentences.n: The clause is built as a cross-pattern round a single verb: object, subject, subject, object — “pietatem (object) publica causa (subject) rexque (subject) patrem (object) vicit”. Both defeats happen inside one man: the public interest overcomes “pietas”, the duty owed to one's own blood, and the king overcomes the father. “datura” is the future participle, “on the point of giving”; “castum … cruorem” picks up the “sanguine virgineo” of the seer's words. “flentibus … ministris” is an ablative absolute, “with the attendants weeping”, and it is the only grief this sentence records. Iphigenia is named here and nowhere else in the part.

sentences.t:
victa dea est nubemque oculis obiecit et inter
officium turbamque sacri vocesque precantum
supposita fertur mutasse Mycenida cerva.
sentences.l:
the goddess was conquered, and threw a cloud before their eyes, and amid
the rite and the crowd of the sacrifice and the voices of those praying
she is said to have exchanged the girl of Mycenae, a hind being put in her place.
sentences.i: the goddess gave way; she threw a cloud over their eyes, and in the middle of the ceremony, the press of the sacrifice and the voices of the praying, she is said to have swapped the girl of Mycenae for a hind set in her place.
sentences.n: “victa … est” answers the “vicit” two lines above: what conquered the father is now matched by the goddess conquered in her turn, the same verb turned round. “mutasse” is syncopated for “mutavisse”. “supposita … cerva” is ablative and works two ways at once — “with a hind substituted” (absolute) and “exchanged for a hind” (the ablative that goes with “mutare”); the translations keep both. “Mycenida” is a Greek accusative, the woman of Mycenae. “fertur”, “she is said”, holds the rescue at arm's length as what people tell — and the cloud has already made sure nobody at the altar saw it.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi, qua decuit, lenita est caede Diana,
et pariter Phoebes, pariter maris ira recessit,
accipiunt ventos a tergo mille carinae
multaque perpessae Phrygia potiuntur harena.
sentences.l:
Therefore when Diana had been softened by the killing by which it was fitting,
and equally the anger of Phoebe, equally that of the sea, withdrew,
the thousand keels take the winds at their backs
and, having endured much, take possession of the Phrygian sand.
sentences.i: So, when Diana had been appeased by the killing that was owed her, and the anger of Phoebe and the anger of the sea alike went down, the thousand ships took the wind astern and, having borne much, made the Phrygian shore.
sentences.n: “qua decuit … caede” — “by the killing by which it was fitting”: the edition's commas set off the little relative clause “qua decuit”, which stands ahead of its own noun, so the reader meets “by which” before “by the killing”; both are ablative because each clause wants an ablative of means of its own. The phrase is chilling in its flatness, calling the killing simply the proper one. “Phoebes” is the Greek genitive of Phoebe, Diana under her other name, so the goddess is named twice in two lines and her anger set beside the sea's. “perpessae” is the participle of a deponent verb and so active in force — the ships having endured, not having been endured. “potiuntur” takes the ablative “harena”. “carinae”, keels, is the ship named by its part.

sentences.t:
Orbe locus medio est inter terrasque fretumque
caelestesque plagas, triplicis confinia mundi,
unde quod est usquam, quamvis regionibus absit,
inspicitur, penetratque cavas vox omnis ad aures.
sentences.l:
There is a place in the middle of the world, between the lands and the sea
and the tracts of heaven, the shared borders of the threefold universe,
from which whatever is anywhere, however far off in its own region,
is looked into, and every voice makes its way through to hollow ears.
sentences.i: There is a place at the middle of the world, between land and sea and the regions of the sky, where the three parts of the universe meet; from it whatever exists anywhere, however far away it lies, can be seen into, and every voice finds its way through to hollow ears.
sentences.n: “Orbe … medio” is ablative of place without a preposition. “triplicis confinia mundi” stands in apposition to “locus”: a “confinium” is the border two territories share, so the place is where earth, sea and sky all touch — not a centre so much as a common frontier. “quod est usquam” (“whatever is anywhere”) is the subject of “inspicitur”, and “inspicitur” is stronger than “is seen”: it is looked into, examined. “quamvis … absit” concedes the distance with the subjunctive, “however far off it may be”. The place is built out of position alone; there is no landscape in it at all.

sentences.t:
Fama tenet summaque domum sibi legit in arce,
innumerosque aditus ac mille foramina tectis
addidit et nullis inclusit limina portis:
sentences.l:
Rumour holds it, and chose herself a house on the topmost height,
and countless ways in and a thousand openings to the building
she added, and shut in the thresholds with no doors:
sentences.i: Rumour holds the place, and picked out a house for herself on its highest point; she put countless approaches into the building and a thousand openings, and closed no threshold with a door:
sentences.n: “Fama” is Rumour — report, talk, what is said — the personified power, not fame in the modern sense of celebrity; everything described from here on is a building made to let sound in and out. “sibi legit” is “chose for herself”, and “legit” is perfect, matching “addidit”. “nullis inclusit limina portis” states by a negative what a door is for: the thresholds are shut in by no doors at all. An “arx” is a citadel, the high defended point of a city — the word puts Rumour where a stronghold would sit.

sentences.t: nocte dieque patet.
sentences.l: By night and by day it stands open.
sentences.i: It is open night and day.
sentences.n: Three words, and the architecture is explained: “patet” is the verb of a door standing open, and the ablatives “nocte dieque” mark the time within which. The short sentence lands after a long one and stops the description dead for a moment before the noise starts.

sentences.t:
Tota est ex aere sonanti,
tota fremit vocesque refert iteratque quod audit.
sentences.l:
The whole of it is of sounding bronze;
the whole roars, and carries voices back and repeats what it hears.
sentences.i: The house is bronze throughout, and the bronze rings; the whole of it roars, throws voices back and says again whatever it hears.
sentences.n: The repeated “tota” — once for the material, once for the noise — makes the two the same fact; the second of them opens the line. “ex aere sonanti” is made out of resounding bronze, the metal of gongs and echoing halls. “refert” is “carries back”, the verb of an echo, and “iterat” is simply “does again”. The house is described entirely by what happens to sound inside it.

sentences.t:
Nulla quies intus nullaque silentia parte,
nec tamen est clamor, sed parvae murmura vocis,
qualia de pelagi, siquis procul audiat, undis
esse solent, qualemve sonum, cum Iuppiter atras
increpuit nubes, extrema tonitrua reddunt.
sentences.l:
No rest inside, and silence in no part,
yet there is no shouting, but the murmurs of a small voice,
such as are wont to come from the waves of the sea, should someone
hear them from far off, or such a sound as, when Jupiter has rattled
the black clouds, the last thunders give back.
sentences.i: There is no rest inside, and no quiet anywhere in it; and yet there is no shouting either, only the murmuring of a small voice — the sound the sea's waves have when you hear them from a distance, or the sound the last of the thunder gives back when Jupiter has cracked the black clouds.
sentences.n: “silentia” is plural, “silences”, and “nulla … parte” is ablative, “in no quarter of it”. The double comparison runs on two heads, “qualia” and “qualem”: first the sea heard from far off, then thunder dying away. “siquis procul audiat” is dropped in as a parenthesis with the subjunctive of a supposed case, “if anyone should hear”. “increpuit” is transitive here — Jupiter rattles the clouds — and “extrema tonitrua” are the last rolls, the rumble after the crack. Both comparisons pick sound at its faintest: what is being described is not volume but a low continuous massed noise.

sentences.t: Atria turba tenet:
sentences.l: A crowd holds the halls:
sentences.i: A crowd fills the entrance halls:
sentences.n: “atria” are the great front rooms of a Roman house, where callers waited and business was done — Rumour's house is laid out on the plan of a rich man's. “tenet” is the same verb used above of Rumour holding the place, now transferred to the crowd that has taken over her hall.

sentences.t:
veniunt, leve vulgus, euntque
mixtaque cum veris passim commenta vagantur
milia rumorum confusaque verba volutant.
sentences.l:
they come — a light crowd — and they go,
and everywhere fictions mixed with true things wander about,
thousands of rumours, and they roll jumbled words around.
sentences.i: they come and go, a flighty crowd; made-up things mixed in with true ones drift about everywhere, thousands of rumours, and they keep turning muddled words over and over.
sentences.n: “leve vulgus” is dropped in between “veniunt” and “euntque” and comments on the coming and going: “levis” is light in weight and so unsteady, fickle. “commenta” are things invented, made up. The syntax leaves “milia rumorum” free to be read either as a further subject of “vagantur” (wander) or as the subject of “volutant” (roll about); the translations attach it to the wandering and let the same word carry on into the next verb. “volutant” is frequentative — rolling done over and over.

sentences.t:
E quibus hi vacuas inplent sermonibus aures,
hi narrata ferunt alio;
sentences.l:
Of whom these fill empty ears with talk,
those carry the things told elsewhere;
sentences.i: Some of them fill idle ears with talk; others carry what they were told off to somewhere else;
sentences.n: “hi … hi” is “some … others”. “vacuas … aures” are empty ears, with nothing in them yet and so ready to be filled. “inplent” keeps the edition's unassimilated spelling of “implent” and is not damage. “narrata” is the neuter plural participle used as a noun, “the things that have been told”. “alio” is the adverb “to another place”, not a form of “alius” agreeing with anything.

sentences.t:
mensuraque ficti
crescit, et auditis aliquid novus adicit auctor.
sentences.l:
and the measure of the falsehood
grows, and each new teller adds something to what he has heard.
sentences.i: and the falsehood grows in measure, and each new teller adds something to what he was told.
sentences.n: “ficti” is another participle used as a noun, “of the thing made up”, and “mensura” is a measure taken, so the invention has a size that increases with each passing on. “auditis” is dative plural neuter, “to the things heard”, governed by “adicit”, which adds one thing to another. An “auctor” is the person a report can be traced back to, so “novus auctor” is the fresh authority — and the point is that each new authority adds what has no authority behind it. The tense is present and general: this is how it always goes.

sentences.t:
Illic Credulitas, illic temerarius Error
vanaque Laetitia est consternatique Timores
Seditioque recens dubioque auctore Susurri.
sentences.l:
There is Credulity, there rash Error
and empty Joy and panic-stricken Fears
and freshly risen Sedition and Whisperings whose author is uncertain.
sentences.i: There live Credulity, and reckless Error, and groundless Joy, and Fears in a panic, and Sedition newly risen, and Whispers with an uncertain source.
sentences.n: The edition capitalises these because they are inhabitants: abstractions housed as persons. Singulars (Credulitas, Error, Laetitia, Seditio) stand beside plurals (Timores, Susurri) — fears and whispers come in numbers. “est” is singular although the list is long, agreeing with the nearest item. “consternati” is used of a herd or a crowd panicked into stampede. “dubio … auctore” is an ablative of description going with the Whisperings, “of doubtful source”, and it picks up “auctor” from just above, where the new teller was the source; a whisper is a report that has lost its author. Magnus prints “recens”, “newly risen”; some editions print “repens”, “sudden”.

sentences.t:
Ipsa, quid in caelo rerum pelagoque geratur
et tellure, videt totumque inquirit in orbem.
sentences.l:
She herself sees what of matters is being carried on in the sky and the sea
and the land, and searches into the whole world.
sentences.i: Rumour herself sees whatever is going on in sky and sea and land, and pushes her search out over the whole world.
sentences.n: “quid … rerum geratur” is an indirect question and so takes the subjunctive “geratur”; “quid rerum” is a partitive genitive, “what of matters”. The three ablatives are split across the line-break, so that the last of them, “et tellure”, opens the following line after sky and sea have already been named. “inquirit in orbem” is the verb of an investigation aimed into something: Rumour does not merely receive what comes to her — she goes looking.
